subtitulo: Otto of Bavaria, Athens as capital, and the invention of public employment as political currency (1832–1864)

coda.heading: Coda for the trip: what to look at

items.text: In Athens, walk the full length of Panepistimiou Street and look at the neoclassical trilogy knowing it is an ideological set built by Scandinavians. Then go into Plaka and Anafiotika, the whitewashed neighborhood built by masons brought from the island of Anafi to raise the royal palace: a piece of Cycladic architecture climbing the slope of the Acropolis, illegal, tolerated, and today one of the most photographed corners of the city. The official capital and the capital of those who built it, two hundred meters apart.

In Corfu, the Palace of St. Michael and St. George, at the northern end of the Esplanade, seat of the British Lord High Commissioner, today a museum of Asian art. And the British cemetery. And cricket. Watch how the island narrates its British period: with ironic distance, with selective nostalgia, almost never as domination. Compare that with how it narrates the Venetian period. And compare it, above all, with how Peru narrates its own nineteenth-century British presence — the railways, the Grace Contract, the trading houses — which was a form of economic control without a flag, and precisely for that reason is rarely named as imperialism.

sections.heading: A seventeen-year-old king and a foreign regency
paragraphs: Otto of Wittelsbach landed at Nafplio in February 1833 at seventeen years of age, with three Bavarian regents, Bavarian officials, and some three thousand five hundred Bavarian soldiers paid for by the loan guaranteed by the powers. He was Catholic in an Orthodox country, did not speak Greek on arrival, and had no constitutional obligation whatsoever: he reigned as an absolute monarch because London, Paris, and St. Petersburg had arranged it that way.

The Bavarian regency did, within a few years, what no Greek power had managed to do: it built a state. Legal codes based on German and French models, a hierarchical judicial system, prefectures, a regular army that disbanded the irregular bands, a national bank, the University of Athens in 1837, and the unilateral proclamation of the autocephaly of the Greek Church in 1833, subordinating it to the state and dissolving hundreds of small monasteries to seize their assets.

And it produced, simultaneously, deep rejection. The fighters of the revolution were left out of the new army; the notables, out of the new bureaucracy; the Church, subordinated; and the expense of the court and the imported administration proved disproportionate for a ruined country. Kolokotronis was condemned to death in 1834 in a political trial, then pardoned. The hero of independence prosecuted by the state his war had made possible: the image encapsulates the entire relationship between revolution and order.

The relevant Peruvian comparison is not with an imported king but with something subtler: the adoption of European codes, constitutions, and institutional models over societies whose actual structure did not correspond to them. Peru promulgated liberal constitutions throughout the nineteenth century while most of its population remained outside effective citizenship by census, literacy, and language requirements. An imported institution is not implanted in a vacuum: it is superimposed on the existing structure and produces a dual regime, with modern formal rules and a real, patrimonial functioning underneath. Greece and Peru are two classic cases of that duality, and it is probably the trait they share most.

sections.heading: Athens as capital: a village chosen for its name
paragraphs: In 1834 the capital moved from Nafplio to Athens. The decision deserves attention because it is purely symbolic and its consequences were enormous. Athens was then a small settlement, numbering a few thousand inhabitants, damaged by the war, with no working port, insufficient water, no industry, and no commercial importance. Thessaloniki, Patras, or Nafplio itself were materially superior options. Athens was chosen because it was called Athens.

What followed was an exercise in ideological urbanism: an orthogonal plan designed by the architects Kleanthis and Schaubert, corrected by the Bavarian Klenze, with axes that visually framed the Acropolis; the neoclassical trilogy on Panepistimiou Street built by Danish and German architects; and an archaeological policy that consisted of clearing the Acropolis of everything later than Antiquity — the Frankish tower, the Ottoman structures, the mosque installed inside the Parthenon — to restore a classical state that had never existed in that form. The new state sculpted its capital as an argument.

And the argument worked, in the sense that Athens grew until it now concentrates more than a third of the country's population. Greece is, like Peru, a state with extreme MACROCEPHALY: a capital that absorbs population, investment, administration, and opportunities, while the interior empties out. Lima concentrates around a third of Peruvians for different reasons — colonial centralism and later migration forced by violence and lack of opportunity — but the morphological result is the same, and so are its political effects: the distance between capital and hinterland becomes a distance of representation, and much of the political crisis of both countries is explained by that fracture.

sections.heading: Autochthons and heterochthons: the fight over state jobs
paragraphs: Here is the central finding of this installment, and probably one of the most useful in the whole plan.

The new kingdom was poor: subsistence agriculture, no industry, no capital, with commerce controlled by Greeks who lived outside its borders. In that context, PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT became the country's principal distributable economic resource. And since more than two-thirds of Greeks lived outside the kingdom, and many of the best educated — Phanariots, diaspora merchants, Ionians — flocked to the new state to occupy posts, a conflict erupted that dominated politics in the 1840s: that of AUTOCHTHONS versus HETEROCHTHONS, those born within the borders against those who had arrived from outside. The constitution of 1844, wrested from the king by the military coup of September 3, 1843, included clauses restricting heterochthons' access to public office.

Consider what this means. The first great political fracture of independent Greece was not left against right, nor monarchy against republic: it was a dispute over the distribution of administrative posts, between two factions of the same nation defined by place of birth. And that dispute fixed the structural trait of Greek politics down to the present: parties as PUBLIC-EMPLOYMENT DISTRIBUTION MACHINES, the vote as exchange for placement, and an administration that grows for political rather than functional reasons. In the 1980s and 1990s, every alternation between PASOK and New Democracy entailed a massive rotation of posts. When the troika demanded in 2010 that public employment be reduced, it was not touching a technical inefficiency: it was dismantling the country's central mechanism of political intermediation. That is why it was so explosive.

The Peruvian version exists and works the same way, though with a smaller public sector: the confidence positions that rotate entirely with each government, service contracting that allows patronage placement without competitive examination, the capture of regional bodies, and a civil service career that gets reformed on paper every decade without ever being implemented. In both countries the moralizing critique — "politicians hand out jobs" — explains nothing. What explains it is this: where the state is the principal accessible formal employer and the private economy offers no mobility, the public post is the political good par excellence, and whoever controls its distribution controls politics. Changing that requires changing the economic structure, not exhorting virtue.

sections.heading: The Megali Idea: an impossible foreign policy
paragraphs: In January 1844, during the constitutional debates, Prime Minister Ioannis Kolettis delivered the speech that gave the doctrine its name: the kingdom of Greece is not Greece, he said; Greece is also Constantinople, Thessaloniki, Trebizond, Crete, Samos, and every land where Greeks live. The MEGALI IDEA, the Great Idea, was thereby formulated as a national program: to reunite in a single state all the Greeks of the old Byzantine space.

Note the program's internal function. Kolettis formulated it, among other things, to resolve the dispute between autochthons and heterochthons: if the state is provisional and its destiny is to encompass everyone, the distinction between those born inside and outside loses its meaning. External irredentism as a solution to an internal distributive conflict. It is a frequent mechanism, and it is worth keeping in mind whenever a government in difficulty discovers a national cause at the border.

The consequences were disastrous and took eighty years to fully manifest. The Megali Idea committed a small, indebted, industry-less state to a permanent expansionist foreign policy that cost it wars in 1897 — a humiliating defeat against the Ottomans — in 1912–1913, in 1917–1918, and finally in 1919–1922, when the attempt to annex western Anatolia ended in the disaster we will see in Block IV. Each expansion demanded more debt and more militarization, and each failure produced internal political crisis.

The Peruvian equivalent of this logic is the relationship between territorial national project and state capacity in the nineteenth century: the War of the Pacific of 1879–1883 found a bankrupt country — it had suspended payments in 1876 after the exhaustion of the guano cycle — sustaining an international position that its finances and its state could not back. The defeat was military, and before that, it was fiscal. Greece would live its exact equivalent in 1897 and in 1922.

sections.heading: 1862–1864: one king leaves, another arrives, and the Ionians change hands
paragraphs: Otto was deposed by a military pronouncement and an uprising in October 1862, after thirty years of reign, without an heir and worn down by economic crisis and by his failure to expand the borders. The powers chose a successor: Prince William of Denmark, seventeen years old — the same age Otto had been on arrival — who reigned as George I for fifty years.

And here your own destination enters the story. As an incentive for Greece to accept the British candidate and to consolidate the new dynasty, Great Britain ceded to Greece in 1864 the United States of the Ionian Islands, which it had administered since 1815. That is: Corfu, Paxos, Zakynthos, Cephalonia, and the other islands were incorporated into Greece as a DIPLOMATIC GIFT tied to a change of dynasty, not by conquest or by their own decision — although the local unionist movement had been pressing for decades and several of its leaders had been persecuted by the British administration.

The British condition was significant: Corfu's fortifications had to be dismantled and the islands declared permanently neutral, so that no other power could use them. The British blew up part of the defenses before leaving. They left behind, instead, roads, the aqueduct system, the Palace of St. Michael and St. George, cricket, and a tradition of ginger beer still drunk on the island.

The incorporation also produced a real social shock: the Ionians arrived with a university, codes, a press, a registered nobility, and an Italian-speaking elite, into a kingdom that was poorer and less institutionalized. For decades, Ionians were overrepresented in Greek administration, the judiciary, and culture. When someone in Corfu tells you the island "was always different," the claim has a precise and verifiable historical basis, and it is not merely local pride.

sections.heading: The simultaneous world and resonances, 2024–2026
paragraphs: These decades are those of Italian unification in 1861 and German unification in 1871, the American Civil War, the opening of Japan and the Meiji Restoration of 1868, the Taiping Rebellion in China — perhaps twenty million dead — and, in Peru, the guano era, with extraordinary fiscal revenues between 1840 and 1879, the abolition of slavery and of indigenous tribute in 1854, the arrival of Chinese laborers under semi-servile contracts, and the massive external indebtedness that would lead to the bankruptcy of 1876. Greece and Peru, once again, in the same rhythm: both building a state on credit.

The sharpest contemporary resonance is public employment as a political resource, which remains structural in both countries and which in Greece went through a decade of forced dismantling between 2010 and 2018, with very severe cuts to staff and salaries, and an unresolved debate about how a capable administration is rebuilt afterward. The second resonance is macrocephaly: in 2024–2026 Athens concentrates population, impossible rents, and tourist pressure, while the periphery depopulates and regional politics is reduced to chasing European funds. Replace "European funds" with "mining royalties" and you have the Peruvian debate on decentralization, which for twenty years has been producing regional governments with resources and without capacity, and which is one of the country's least evaluated reforms.
